Chapters 5A & 5B

Temporary Speed Reductions & Environmental Zones

Emergency speed limits during an oil crisis, and the rules governing low-emission and zero-emission zones in Dutch cities.

  • Chapter 5A — Oil Crisis Speed Limits
  • Chapter 5B — Environmental Zones

These two short chapters address situations where the standard traffic rules are modified — either temporarily in a national emergency, or permanently in designated urban zones. Neither chapter is heavily tested in the theory exam, but both reflect important aspects of how Dutch traffic law adapts to real-world conditions: energy crises, air quality, and the transition to zero-emission transport.

Chapter 5A — Temporary Speed Reduction in an Oil Supply Crisis

Emergency provisions that allow the government to lower speed limits nationally when oil supply is severely disrupted.

The Legal Basis Emergency power

Chapter 5A gives the Dutch government a specific legal tool: in the event of a serious disruption to oil supply — a national energy crisis — the Minister of Infrastructure and Water Management can issue a decree temporarily lowering speed limits across the entire country.

This provision was originally created in response to the 1973 oil crisis, when the Netherlands — like many countries — introduced emergency Sunday driving bans and lower speed limits to conserve fuel. The legal framework remains in the RVV 1990 as a precautionary tool.

Emergency Speed Reduction Powers

If activated, the decree can lower the standard speed limits to the following reduced levels across all Dutch roads:

130
Normal motorway
→
100
Emergency motorway limit
80
Normal rural road
→
80
Unchanged

The exact limits are set by ministerial decree at the time of the crisis. The reduced limits apply from the moment the decree is published.

How the Reduction Is Announced Publication

When the Minister activates the emergency speed reduction, it is announced through an official government decree published in the Staatscourant (the Dutch Official Gazette). From the moment of publication, the lower limits are legally binding — even before new signs are placed on the road.

In practice, reduced speed limit signs are placed on motorways as quickly as possible to make the change visible to drivers. The announcement is also widely covered in news media.

Duration and End of the Measure Temporary

The emergency speed reduction is temporary by design. It remains in force only for as long as the oil supply crisis continues. When the crisis is resolved, the Minister issues a new decree lifting the measure, and the standard speed limits return immediately upon publication of that decree.

During the period of reduced limits, all normal enforcement mechanisms apply — speed cameras, police checks and fines all operate against the reduced limits, not the standard ones.

This chapter has never been used since its original creation in the 1970s context. It remains in the law as a contingency. Its practical relevance for the theory exam is limited — understand the concept, not the detail.
For the Theory Exam

Chapter 5A is rarely tested in depth. The key facts to know are: the emergency speed reduction can be activated by ministerial decree during an oil crisis, it lowers speed limits nationally, and it is temporary — lifted when the crisis ends. You do not need to memorise specific reduced limit numbers for the exam.

Chapter 5B — Environmental Zones & Zero-Emission Zones

The rules governing milieuzone (low-emission zones) and nul-emissiezone (zero-emission zones) — where they apply, which vehicles are affected, and what the exemptions are.

Why Environmental Zones Exist Air quality

Environmental zones are areas within cities where access by certain older or more polluting vehicles is restricted or prohibited. They exist to improve air quality in densely populated urban areas where traffic emissions significantly affect public health.

Dutch municipalities have the authority to designate their own zones — the RVV 1990 provides the legal framework, but each city decides whether to implement zones and defines their boundaries. Amsterdam, Utrecht, Rotterdam and many other cities have active environmental zones.

The Two Types of Zone

🌿
Milieuzone

A low-emission zone that restricts access for vehicles that do not meet a minimum emission standard. The focus is on older diesel vehicles — passenger cars, vans and trucks — that produce significantly higher levels of particulate matter and nitrogen oxides.

Which emission standard is required varies by city and is updated over time as standards tighten. Vehicles must meet the required Euro emission class to enter freely.

  • Sign: green square with "Milieuzone" text and leaf symbol
  • Applies at the point of entry — no advance notice required
  • Monitored by camera systems reading number plates
⚡
Nul-emissiezone

A zero-emission zone that allows only vehicles producing zero exhaust emissions — primarily fully electric vehicles. All combustion-engine vehicles (petrol, diesel, LPG) are excluded unless they hold a valid exemption or waiver.

Zero-emission zones are being introduced in stages across Dutch city centres, primarily targeting freight delivery vehicles first, with passenger vehicles following in later phases.

  • Sign: blue square with "Nul-emissiezone" text and plug symbol
  • Stricter than a milieuzone — zero tailpipe emissions required
  • Monitored by camera systems
Which Vehicles Are Affected Targeted vehicle types

The zones primarily target motor vehicles with combustion engines that do not meet the required emission standard. The specific vehicles affected depend on the zone type and local rules, but the general pattern is:

  • Milieuzone: Older diesel passenger cars, diesel vans, diesel trucks — typically those that do not meet Euro 4 (passenger cars) or Euro 6 (trucks/vans) standards, depending on the city and year
  • Nul-emissiezone: All combustion-engine vehicles — petrol, diesel, LPG — unless specifically exempted
  • Bicycles, e-bikes, electric vehicles: Always permitted in both zone types
  • Mopeds and motorcycles: Generally not subject to zone restrictions unless a local decision specifically includes them

Built-in Exemptions — Who May Always Enter

🚨 Emergency vehicles

Ambulances, fire trucks, police vehicles and other emergency services are always exempt — regardless of emission class or fuel type.

♿ Adapted vehicles

Vehicles specifically adapted for disabled persons (e.g. wheelchair-accessible vehicles with adaptation code) may enter zone-restricted areas.

🏕️ Camper vans

Camper vans registered as such have a specific exemption in the milieuzone — they may enter to park and unpack at their home address. This exemption does not apply in nul-emissiezones.

🏛️ Historic vehicles

Vehicles 40 years or older are exempt from zone restrictions — they are considered heritage vehicles, not typical daily transport.

🚌 Public transport

Licensed public transport vehicles (buses, trams) are exempt from zone restrictions regardless of emission class, as they operate under separate environmental frameworks.

🪖 Military vehicles

Military vehicles operated by the Dutch armed forces are exempt from environmental zone restrictions when on official duty.

Ontheffing — Individual Exemption Permits Application required

Beyond the automatic exemptions above, vehicle owners who do not meet the emission requirements can apply to the relevant municipality for an individual exemption permit (ontheffing). These are typically granted for:

  • Vehicles used for essential services with no electric alternative available
  • Business vehicles making occasional deliveries — sometimes a day pass system is offered
  • Vehicles that are being replaced imminently
  • Special operational needs that cannot be met by compliant vehicles

Exemption permits are time-limited and must be renewed. They are issued by the municipality, not by national government.

A common day-pass system exists for trucks: vehicles that enter a zero-emission zone no more than 12 times per year per municipality can apply for a daily permit. This allows occasional access without requiring full compliance.
How Zones Are Enforced Camera enforcement

Environmental and zero-emission zones are enforced entirely by automatic camera systems. Cameras at zone entry points read number plates and check them automatically against the vehicle registration database. Vehicles that do not meet the requirements and do not hold a valid permit receive a fine automatically — there is no need for a police officer to be present.

The fine is sent to the registered owner of the vehicle. Foreign vehicles are also checked — number plates from other EU countries can be matched against foreign vehicle databases through international agreements.

Zone Signs — How to Recognise Them Visual recognition

Environmental zones are marked with specific signs at all entry points. The signs indicate:

  • Start of zone: Square sign with zone name and applicable vehicle categories — green background for milieuzone, blue background for nul-emissiezone
  • End of zone: Same sign with a diagonal red line through it
  • Supplementary boards: May specify which vehicle types are affected, time periods, or exemption conditions

Inside a zone, reminder signs are often placed at major junctions. If you are approaching a city centre, watch for zone entry signs well before you enter — turning around inside a zone is inconvenient and may require using restricted roads.

Milieuzone vs Nul-emissiezone — Side by Side

Feature Milieuzone Nul-emissiezone
Goal Reduce particulate matter and NOx from older vehicles Eliminate all exhaust emissions in the zone
Who is excluded Vehicles below a minimum Euro emission class All combustion-engine vehicles (unless exempt)
Electric vehicles Always permitted Always permitted
Hybrids Usually permitted if Euro class is met Only if zero tailpipe emissions (plug-in hybrids in electric mode only in some cases)
Sign colour Green Blue
Enforcement Automatic camera — number plate recognition Automatic camera — number plate recognition
Individual permit possible Yes — from municipality Yes — from municipality, stricter conditions
Current phase Active in many cities Being rolled out — freight first, then passenger vehicles
Planning a Trip Through a Dutch City

Before driving into any major Dutch city, check whether your vehicle is subject to environmental zone restrictions. The RDW website (rdw.nl) allows you to look up your number plate and see whether your vehicle meets the requirements for active zones. Most navigation apps now also display zone boundaries and can route you around them if needed.

Zones Are Local — Rules Vary by City

While the RVV 1990 provides the legal framework, the actual zone boundaries, the specific emission classes required and the exemption rules are set by each municipality separately. Amsterdam's milieuzone may have different requirements from Utrecht's. Always check the specific city's rules before entering — do not assume one city's rules apply everywhere.

Chapters 5A & 5B — What to Take Away

Chapter 5A gives the government emergency powers to temporarily lower speed limits nationally during an oil supply crisis. It is activated by ministerial decree, applies immediately, and is lifted when the crisis ends. It has rarely been used in practice.

Chapter 5B establishes the legal framework for environmental zones. A milieuzone restricts older polluting vehicles. A nul-emissiezone allows only zero-emission vehicles. Both are enforced by cameras. Emergency vehicles, historic vehicles (40+ years), adapted disability vehicles and public transport are always exempt. Individual permits can be applied for from the municipality.

For the exam: know the difference between milieuzone and nul-emissiezone, know the automatic exemption categories, and understand that zones are set by municipalities — not nationally uniform.
